origins: Pain that lasts for months or years teaches the mind to expect only more pain. Each flare confirms the fear, and hope for relief becomes dangerous. Sleep loss and worry magnify the experience.
teaches: The psalmist cries, “How long, O LORD?” and later says, “I will sing to the LORD, for He has been good to me” (Psalm 13). “For He has not despised or detested the torment of the afflicted. He has not hidden His face from him, but has attended to his cry for help.” “Weeping may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning.” We cannot promise relief, but we can say that God hears, that you are not alone in the pain, and that today’s suffering is not the whole story.
self_statements: It will always be like this.
I cannot survive more years of this.
errors: Believing pain is either gone or forever.
Feeling pain intensely and concluding it will not end.
Calling myself a person in permanent pain.
questions: What patterns do I notice in my pain, such as better and worse times?
What has helped even a little?
Who is on my care team, and have I told them everything?
How have I coped before when pain eased?
What does God do with the cry “How long?”
What can I do today to make today a bit more bearable?
truth: God hears my cry and does not despise my pain. I cannot see the end, but I can take today one hour at a time, use every wise help available, and trust that He is with me.
hw_truths: God has not despised my torment.
He attends to my cry for help.
Weeping may last the night; joy comes.
The Lord is near to the brokenhearted.
His mercies are new each morning.
log: Each day, note one thing that eased the pain a little.
prayer: Lord, the pain is wearing me down. You do not despise my suffering. Hear my cry, give strength for today, and lead me to the help I need. Amen.
